items.title: Apple plans fix as Microsoft's Exchange shutdown disrupts Mac email
items.content_html:
Apple is working on a fix for Exchange access in its Mac apps as Microsoft retires the connection they rely on.

The disruption concerns work or school accounts hosted through Microsoft's Exchange Online service. This can disrupt Mail, Calendar, Contacts, Notes, and Reminders, while Apple prepares an update and administrators retain temporary options.

A reader from Old Dominion University forwarded an IT notice reporting problems accessing university email through Apple's built-in Mail app. The notice recommends Mac users switch to Outlook and says iPhone and iPad apps are unaffected.

The problem involves Exchange Online, Microsoft's cloud service for workplace and school email, calendars, and other account information. Apple's Mac apps access that information through Exchange Web Services (EWS), an older connection method Microsoft began disabling in October 2026.

Any organization using this connection can face similar problems, depending on their settings. Microsoft says administrators can temporarily keep approved apps connected before Microsoft fully shuts down EWS in April 2027.

The change affects the connection used by Apple's Mac apps. iPhones and iPads use Exchange ActiveSync, a different connection method unaffected by the EWS shutdown.

Apple says a future macOS 27 update will move all five affected Mac apps to Microsoft's replacement connection method. Apple has not announced when that update will arrive.

items.title: iPhone Duo inner display has a replaceable $19 top layer
items.content_html:
AppleCare coverage for the iPhone Duo will mean inexpensive repairs for Apple's first foldable, including $99 full inner display replacement or $19 "cover layer" swaps.

Apple's iPhone Duo may be the most complex and expensive iPhone to date, but thankfully it appears to be inexpensive to repair. At least, that will be the case if you have AppleCare.

According to Apple's service and repair website, first discovered by Quinn Nelson of SnazzyLabs, the iPhone Duo has a swappable cover layer that will cost just $19 with active AppleCare coverage. Of course, this will mean going to an Authorized Apple Service Provider to get it done.

Other AppleCare repair costs include $29 for front display or back glass repairs and a $99 inner display repair. Accidental damage repair is also $99 and theft or loss replacement is $149.

An interview with Apple's VP of hardware engineering Kate Bergeron, shared by 9to5Mac, reveals that Apple's intention with the removable cover layer is an option for user replacement after wearing in the existing layer. She said that Apple engineered the cover layer to wear in for as long as possible before a user might need to replace it.

Since we're talking AppleCare, that means that the layer likely isn't meant to be "user" replaceable, though we won't know how easy it is to get off or put a new one back on until testing can be done. There is a small chance that Apple's self-service website will provide users a path to purchasing their own display cover layer.

AppleCare coverage for iPhone Duo will be much cheaper than paying for repairs without it

If it is easily peeled off, there is also an opportunity for third-party alternative outer layers. I could imagine different textures for Apple Pencil, privacy layers, or glossy covers that are more durable overall.

Obviously, Apple has engineered iPhone Duo and its hinge mechanism to account for the exact thickness and material of its first-party cover layer. Knowing Apple, this isn't some kind of simple screen protector-like surface and isn't intended for novice user replacement or third-party alternatives.

Going without one likely isn't an option either.

Whatever the case, wait to let the YouTubers with too much time and money to break a few iPhone Duos before trying any of this yourself. Chances are that any alternative cover layer could potentially damage the iPhone Duo and even invalidate the warranty and AppleCare.

iPhone Duo goes up for pre-order on October 16 and ships on October 23. It starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage.

items.title: Why I can't wait to swap this iPhone 18 Pro Max for an iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
I've been using an iPhone 18 Pro Max for two weeks, and while it's been great, I'm very much looking forward to it making way for something new and exciting in the brand-new iPhone Duo.

I reviewed the iPhone 18 Pro Max for AppleInsider, giving it a very respectable four stars out of five. At the time I wrote that review, and for the next three weeks as I write this, it's the very best iPhone money can buy.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max has three great cameras, a battery that lasts for far beyond a day, and a huge, gorgeous display. And yet, I find myself wishing for more. Something different from the slab of glass and metal that iPhone owners have become so accustomed to.

That "something different" ships to customers and will pop up at retail on Friday, October 23, 2026. It's called iPhone Duo, and it will bring the biggest change to the iPhone lineup since the iPhone 6 Plus brought us big screens more than a decade ago.

Apple has iterated on the iPhone design for almost 20 years at this point, settling on a form factor that has become the norm for phones everywhere. It's gone through some changes, increasing the screen size and adding new technologies. But it's a familiar design.

Familiarity isn't a bad thing, far from it. Familiarity is warm and comfortable. But those are things that I want from a good winter coat, or a nice pair of shoes, not my premium phone.

To me, familiarity has brought with it a kind of boredom. Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro Max gained the adjustable aperture camera and a super-fast A20 Pro chip, but on the day-to-day, it's identical to the models that came before.

The same can't be said for the iPhone Duo, Apple's first device of any description with a foldable display.

The iPhone Duo, features and all

Samsung, Huawei, Oppo, and other Android phone fans will be quick to point out that folding phones are nothing new, and they're right. I even reviewed one of those Android foldables in 2025. It was great.

But as fond as I was of the Oppo Find N5, it wasn't an iPhone. It ran Android, not iOS, and that was enough to make it a non-starter for me.

The iPhone Duo won't have that problem. And it has the potential to be so much better for it.

I'm a fan of the iPad, whether that's the 13-inch iPad Pro or the entry-level A16 iPad. But I'm particularly fond of the iPad mini.

For me, the iPad mini is the perfect size for the kind of thing I want to use a tablet for. I use my iPhone for general activities, browsing socials, dealing with emails, and whatnot. I use my Mac when I need the bigger screen and a keyboard.

But there's a scenario between the two. A scenario when I want to enjoy a YouTube video on a bigger display than my iPhone can offer, or to have more space to read a website. That's where an iPad mini-sized device really shines.

That's also where I expect the iPhone Duo to show what it's made of. After all, it has a 7.6-inch inner display, a hair smaller than the iPad mini's 8.3-inch panel.

But the iPhone Duo has a secret weapon, something no iPad mini can claim. Something no iPad can boast, for that matter. The iPhone Duo fits in your pocket.

Having an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, just by unfolding it, could be a real game-changer. It's the answer to all those times you wish your iPhone was a little bigger, or you wish you had your iPad with you.

But as was the case when Apple switched to truly big-screen iPhones, and when it launched the iPad in 2010, it needs developers to make it happen.

Whenever Apple releases a new class of product, or significantly changes an existing one, it needs developers to be on board. They are the ones who fill the App Store with the apps that we use every day across iPhone, iPad, and Mac.

But as Apple found with the Apple Vision Pro launch, getting developers to make apps for a new device isn't always easy. That's especially the case with a niche product like a spatial computer or an expensive folding iPhone.

iPhone Duo isn't just open or closed

The good news, developers tell me, is that some apps will just work out of the box. Developers who took their iPhone apps and converted them to universal apps for the iPad and Mac will get a head start.

Developers whose existing iPhone-only apps rely solely on Apple's stock interface building blocks will also likely have little work to do to make them look great on an iPhone Duo. Although that's with the caveat that using the phone partially folded may cause some strange behavior until properly addressed.

But the developers who make some of the best apps, the ones that have unique interfaces, are a different matter. Those apps that bring the Apple whimsy of the early App Store days, you could say. They'll need some work.

Which brings the obvious question of whether they will, or if the iPhone Duo installed base will be too small to warrant the work.

Time will tell, of course. At a $1,999 starting price, I don't think anyone expects the iPhone Duo to be a huge seller compared to, say, the iPhone 18 Pro. But will it sell enough to get developers interested?

That's the unknown, and one that I suspect Apple is well aware of. This isn't its first rodeo.

But there are uncomfortable parallels between the iPhone Duo and Apple Vision Pro. It might be uncharitable to say it, but there's a thin line between a product being a flop and a cult favorite.

There's also a difference between a high-end product launching into a market that's screaming for more, and one that's trying to define a category.

It'll be fascinating to see which side of that the iPhone Duo will fall on. But until then, I'm just looking forward to having an iPad mini I can take anywhere and everywhere.

items.title: M6 Mac mini review: Excellent hardware badly hampered by too-small SSD
items.content_html:
The M6 Mac mini has a faster chip and is solid hardware, but that $899 hurts and there is just not enough storage at that entry price for Apple Intelligence and all of your apps.

I have loved the Mac mini since day one, more than 20 years ago. There has been one in my house consistently since the first G4 model, generally attached to a television, or used as a server, and so forth.

Oddly, the 2026 M6 Mac mini is not the cheapest Mac overall. The MacBook Neo has something to say about that, but that's just not as convenient for my own workflows.

This time around, for the second time, the Apple Silicon Mac mini skipped a generation, and in 2026, the Mac mini is the first to use the new M6 chip. This is good and bad, but more on that in a bit.

Our review covers the base M6 model. It is the version most buyers will choose, and there's a lot to say about that, what you really must add, and what Apple seems to have in mind for the model when $1000 or more of upgrades are added.

The M6 Mac mini keeps the compact shape from the M4. It's a spec-bump update through and through.

That means you get the usual current-gen design, which means that smaller square with rounded corners. It's two inches tall, including the circular foot that also provides ventilation to the unit. The Wi-Fi antenna remains on the base of the unit, for better and worse.

The outside still looks the same as the previous one, including the black Apple logo on the top, as well as the pair of USB-C ports, the headphone jack, and the power indicator at the front.

M6 Mac mini review: A very familiar base

Around the back is an unchanged mix of ports, again without the immediately visible power button. Once again, it's under the back corner of the casing, which caused a stir last time for being a little harder to reach than in previous Mac minis. It was a mistake then, and it's still a mistake now.

That said, if you're the kind of person who puts the Mac to sleep at the end of the working day and doesn't really shut down the Mac mini itself, you may only need to care about the button on a rare occasion.

Really, the only pain point here is that power button. And even then, for most users, it will only be an issue when they actually need to press it.

The headline change, and the only real change of note here, is the M6 chip. It is Apple's first 2-nanometer processor in a desktop Mac.

The CPU has 12 cores in three types. This consists of two super, four performance, and six efficiency cores.

According to Apple, the M6 has a 40% faster CPU than the M4. A lot of this is due to the super cores, which adds two cores to the count versus the M4 version.

The GPU is also more core-heavy than before, with 12 instead of ten cores. The core improvements as well as the quantity stand to give the M6 a big leap in terms of graphical performance.

M6 Mac mini review: A more unusual placement of the compact computer.

That said, the bigger draw here will be in artificial intelligence processing, as the M6 has been practically made for those tasks.

For a start, there's the Neural Engine, which is now a dual 16-core version. That means there are 32 cores instead of 16 cores in previous editions.

Furthermore, each of those 12 GPU cores have Neural Accelerators, which again help with AI-related task processing. It will help your Photos work from a practical standpoint, or any other "neural" tasking.

Apple says that it has four-times faster AI compute capability than the M4. In LM Studio, it can even hit 4.8 times speeds, Apple adds. We never saw that for the base model, but it is faster.

This is all fine and good, but in practice, how much it actually varies depends on your workloads. It is faster than M4 and M5 Pro Mac minis in some workloads, but in other AI workloads, the M5 Pro core count comes ahead.

It isn't quite the AI monster that the Mac Studio has become, it's still a device that's more than capable of chewing away at queries. Still, though. The Mac mini is better used as an inexpensive workstation with Cloud AI compute instead of on-device, especially with the reviewed $899 model.

The base model as reviewed here has 16GB of unified memory. There are options for upgrades to 24GB and 32GB, if you can afford the upgrade costs.

Memory bandwidth is also a real gain this year. The base 16GB runs at 153GB/s, which is up from the 120GB/s of the M4.

The 24GB and 32GB tiers reach 170GB/s.

M6 Mac mini review: Single-core results

In terms of computing grunt, the M6 Mac mini can push out 4,034 on the single-core test of Geekbench 7. It's an improvement of about 23% on the 3,277 of the M4 Mac mini, thanks to the use of a super core.

Likewise, turning to multi-core, the per-core improvement is mixed with the extra cores to give the M6 a score of 22,594. Against the M4 Mac mini's score of 15,337, that's a 47% improvement.

M6 Mac mini review: Multi-core results

Shifting to graphics, and the Metal test is similarly a big generational gain for the M6 over the M4. At 91,087, the M6 is scoring 68% higher than its predecessor.

M6 Mac mini review: Metal results

There's certainly a performance improvement here. It's even to make even M4 Mac mini owners consider a move up.

Connectivity mostly carries over from the M4. The port layout is unchanged front and back, and that's perfectly fine.

There is HDMI and three Thunderbolt 4 ports, which can run at up to 40Gb/s. They're not the Thunderbolt 5 you'd get from the M5 Pro, but it's only a problem if you need that much bandwidth.

They accompany the two USB-C ports at the front, which run at 10Gb/s. Likewise, they could've been Thunderbolt 5, like the M5 Pro, but there has to be some advantage to upgrading.

The Ethernet connection is a quiet improvement here. The gigabit connection has been switched for 2.5Gb Ethernet, which builds in a little network infrastructure future-proofing.

M6 Mac mini review: Rear ports

You can always pay the $100 to get the 10Gb upgrade, but there's less of a need to do that for right now. And, that creeps you even closer to the M5 Pro Mini, or the Mac Studio.

On the wireless side, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 to the party, as well as Bluetooth 6 and Thread. For most, this is still future-proofing. Wi-Fi 7 networks have not yet proliferated, as they can still be very expensive.

The M6 Mac mini can drive up to three external displays, using a combination of Thunderbolt connections and HDMI. It can now support two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port, too.

Support includes variable refresh rates, HDR, and multi-channel audio. Those Thunderbolt 4 connections can support native DisplayPort 1.4 speeds.

The triple screen layout can consist of a pair of 6K 60Hz screens or two 4K 165Hz screens, as well as either a 5K 60Hz monitor over Thunderbolt or 4K 60Hz over HDMI.

If you go for two screens, the maximum limits include one 8K 60Hz screen or 5K 120Hz, or 4K 240Hz, as well as a second 5K or 4K HDMI display.

RAM and SSD industry pricing has hit the Mac mini hard. The base M6 starts at $899.

This is $300 above the M4 model's launch price, and $500 more than what you could buy the older model through MicroCenter for, at this time in 2025. Though, to be fair, we are currently existing in a memory crisis, and so everything electronic is now very expensive.

The memory itself starts at 16GB. An upgrade to 24GB costs another $200. Going to 32GB is a $400 premium over the base model.

Storage starts at that meager and already discussed 256GB, with upgrades ranging from $200 for 512GB to $500 more for 1TB. If you want 2TB, that's $1000 more than the base unit.

This pricing ladder isn't great. The 256GB capacity reviewed here is hampered a bit by slower drive transfer speeds too, with it hitting about 3150 megabytes per second read and write.

The 512GB model, adding that $200, boosts this to about 6300 megabytes per second read and write speeds. This 512GB is really what we consider the bare minimum for the 2026 Mac mini, since Apple Intelligence is no longer optional, and the 20GB or so models will install regardless of your setting.

And, it's not slotted storage, like the M4 Mac mini was, eliminating that option. For budgetary reasons, we do recommend external SSD or hard drive storage

All said, Apple's pricing could've been a lot worse. It's painful for those on tight budgets, but upgrades have always done that, even without memory market shenanigans.

The M6 Mac mini is not as good a processing bargain as the Mac Studio is, but it's also about half the price with some well-selected upgrades at purchase.

As always, consider your workflows. The M6 edges out the M5 family in single-core use. It's hard to recommend the $899 Mac mini M6 configuration with the storage the way it is.

The M6 Mac mini is a familiar box with a faster heart. It's the continuing pattern for Mac upgrades, where Apple makes the engine faster, while keeping everything else almost exactly the same.

It remains an impressive piece of engineering, with a lot of power, in a small space, sipping power the whole while. Price increases aside, that's still very much the case here.

The gains are all inside, and they are real. The CPU, GPU, and AI performance are all welcome jumps, especially for those with Mac Studio dreams but a Mac mini budget.

The video support and faster 2.5Gb Ethernet too good to have.

M6 Mac mini review: Continuing to take up a small amount of desk space.

The catch is that SSD at entry-level and that higher price. At $899, the base model costs $300 more than before, and that's hard to escape.

For first-time buyers, the M6 Mac mini remains an easy recommendation, assuming more SSD space is bought at purchase, if they want something beefy and don't want a MacBook Neo. Upgraders from the M4 should weigh the AI gains against how much is in their wallets.

With Apple Intelligence, 256GB for a Mac mini is just too small. And, on top of that, that configuration is half the speed of the 512GB version.

I do think that the $1099 model with more storage is the better option. That version is a 4 out of 5.

The RAM and Flash commodity pricing is a real problem for the Mac mini. That price increase cannot be ignored. The math on this is enormously different if the 512GB version was $899.

But it isn't. As such, the entry-level M6 Mac mini will be fine for a first desktop, or an adjunct to an iPhone-primary device, because that 256GB storage just cannot be ignored. Most of this target market has mostly single-core loads, and will be perfectly fine with a MacBook Neo, upgraded, for less money.

While it's not my main computer, I'm keeping my M4 Mac mini for what it's being used for. There's just too much of a price premium not to.

As far as my main computer goes. after I sold my M1 Ultra Mac Studio, after much hemming and hawing, I picked the M5 Max Mac Studio instead of a M6 Mac mini with about $1200 in upgrades to get it where I wanted. It was just too close in pricing, with the M5 Max winning the day.

We'll see what happens with Mac mini after the rumored quick jump to M7 in about a year.

Apple's M6 Mac mini has a starting retail price of $899, but Amazon is already offering a discount on the standard configuration at the time of this review. The $20 markdown brings the price of the M6/16GB/256GB spec down to $879.99.

You can compare prices across every configuration in our Mac mini Price Guide, with deals available on numerous models, including storage upgraded ones that we recommend.

items.title: Texas school district turns to Apple as Chromebook repair costs skyrocket
items.content_html:
Aging Chromebooks and mounting repair costs are a driving force behind one Texas school district switching to iPad and Apple's more economical over time MacBook Neo.

Beaumont Independent School District's board approved a four-year, $11.19 million lease for 14,585 Apple devices. The district expects annual payments of about $2.8 million to replace aging equipment used by students and teachers.

The lease, reported by Beaumont Enterprise, includes 4,085 iPads for pre-K through second grade and 9,500 MacBook Neos for older students. Teachers within the school district will receive 1,000 MacBook Neo laptops under the agreement.

Deputy superintendent Rachel Harrah said nearly two-thirds of the district's devices are beyond their recommended life cycle. The district reported more than 6,600 repairs last year and spent nearly $470,000 in repair and support costs across several reporting periods.

Currently, the district primarily uses Chromebooks. Harrah has said current devices are becoming increasingly difficult to repair, with replacement part costs well over $100 per piece in some cases.

"It's almost half a million dollars just supporting a fleet that is barely moving or working," said Harrah.

Additionally, the district is trying to be more forward-thinking. It would rather students get practical experience on devices that are used within the workplace.

"There is not one environment in the workplace that uses a Chromebook," Harrah said.

The district also compared MacBook Neo with Lenovo and Asus models, reporting lower four-year costs for Apple's option. Harrah pointed to 0% laptop financing, 0.99% iPad financing, AppleCare+ access, and potential resale proceeds as reasons for her recommendation.

The first payment will come from district reserves, with later payments drawing on existing revenue and replacement budgets. Officials plan to evaluate the devices after four years and could postpone replacement if their condition allows.

items.title: Optimistic AT&T tells iPhone 18 Pro Max an iOS update will fix call problems
items.content_html:
AT&T has texted customers on iPhone 18 Pro Max, telling them to upgrade to iOS 27.0.1 to fix cellular issues. Users are saying this update doesn't address their problems.

The key problem, believed to affect only a small number of users, is that the iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T may not make or receive calls, nor always send and receive text messages. AT&T has now texted customers telling them to update iOS specifically to fix these issues.

As first spotted by MacRumors, the text message does at least suggest that this update will fix the problem, but AT&T is possibly being a bit hopeful. Apple has released iOS 27.0.1 but has not confirmed that it addresses the call problem.

Apple has not yet publicly acknowledged the issue at all, though. So it's possible that AT&T knows more than Apple has said about its update, but so far at least some users have been disappointed.

"Word on the street was that the iOS 27.0.1 would be addressing this issue," AppleInsider reader Rod Santiano emailed to say, "but alas it... apparently only addresses the Face ID and unresponsive touchscreen issues that have been happening."

"We're still using our iPhone 18s as glorified iPods," he continued.

Santiano says that Apple tested his iPhone 18 Pro Max and found nothing wrong with it, replaced the phone anyway. So far, the replacement iPhone 18 Pro Max is working, too.

The update does appear to be the one Apple was referring to when it said a fix was coming for the separate Face ID rebooting bug.

If you are affected by the iPhone 18 Pro Max call problem, or any other issue on AT&T, be certain to contact support for both the carrier and Apple. AT&T has a device help center, and Apple has a general support page.

items.title: Meta Muse AI reportedly read Mac Messages without consent
items.content_html:
In a completely unsurprising turn of events, Meta's Muse AI is stealing Apple Messages, past and present, and uploading the contents to its cloud, even if explicitly told not to.

If you use Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, or WhatsApp, you've probably been inundated with prompts to try out Meta's next big questionable service: Muse. And it's not like Meta, the parent company of Facebook, has a great track record regarding privacy, safety, or ethics.

If you're not in the know, Muse is Meta's AI agent designed to help with tasks such as researching topics, preparing briefings, and shopping. According to Meta, it runs on a dedicated virtual computer and can use information from connected apps and data sources to tailor its responses.

Meta says that Muse has to obey permissions that users set up. It won't access any data you don't explicitly allow it to access.

Of course, Meta also hedges, a lot, right at the top of the "How Muse works..." page, saying:

"Your Muse can make mistakes or take unexpected actions," Meta says. No kidding.

I've never used Muse, and frankly, I never will. I'll get into why later.

But Jason Aten over at Inc has. What he's learned is, unfortunately, horrifying.

Aten installed Muse on both his iPhone and a Mac mini that he uses to test out various AI agents and tech. It took Meta a single day to begin "helpfully" pitching article ideas based on texts he'd sent to a podcast co-host.

When he asked Muse how it got the information, it said that it read banners from incoming texts. But that's not true, either.

After doing a little digging, Aten says Muse synced 187,000 lines from his Messages database, despite Full Disk Access being off.

A screenshot of a Threads post where Jason Aten shows Muse synced Messages without permission

I'd like you to read that a second time. Meta's similarly named Messenger app didn't get ingested.

Apple's Messages did.

Unless Aten is the most popular person on the face of the planet, I sincerely doubt he'd gotten 187,000 lines of text in roughly 24 hours. What happened is that, without permission, Muse went into the app and downloaded the information.

He had not given Muse permission to access Messages, and full disk access was not enabled. It just went ahead and uploaded those texts anyway.

Muse can take "unexpected actions" indeed.

Ignoring AI ingestion, Meta is not a company I would trust with any private information anyway. It seems that it's in a race to the bottom, primarily with itself.

It was just over a year ago that the company had asked Facebook users for permission to continuously upload their entire camera roll to its cloud. Meta said this was to "create ideas for posts" for its users, and it would analyze the images for time, location, and themes.

I take a lot of pictures of things that I don't want Meta accessing, and you do too. For me, it's nieces, nephews, medical bills, grievous leg wounds, funny vanity license plates, and probably thousands of embarrassing selfies I send my sister.

None of these are intended to be shared with a company that repeatedly steps on any available rake when it comes to privacy issues.

And just under a year ago, we learned that Meta Ray-Ban Display, Meta's take on smart glasses, has been used by many wearers to violate the privacy and safety of anyone around them. There's even an entire smart glasses subculture dedicated to disabling the lights that make it obvious when the wearers are filming.

I'm not entirely sure what Meta's end goal is, other than to figure out how to turn every single person into a perpetual data generation machine for its company.

And the punchline is, this whole Muse debacle is yet another trumpet blaring as we barrel full speed ahead into the oncoming AI privacy apocalypse. At what point is it too late to solve these problems?

If the agents are already blatantly ignoring the guardrails, are we already past the point of no return?

I think what sticks in my craw about this the most is the fact that Meta has ensured that you do not get the option to opt out. No matter who you are, Meta has found a way to harvest your data.

Prompts to download Muse in WhatsApp, Instagram, and an ad for Muse in the iOS App Store

You could never create a single account on a single Meta service, of which there are many, and you still aren't safe. If you're talking to someone who has installed Muse, Meta could, presumably, access, read, analyze, and upload that information to its services.

And this is the point where I need to step back and point out that this isn't just a Meta issue. I'm naming-and-shaming Meta here because we've got countless examples of Meta's tape-and-bubblegum safety guards failing.

But every company that is investing in AI wants carte blanche access to your information. It doesn't matter if it's Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, or even Apple.

Big tech companies want one thing, and it's disgusting.

I mean, hell, Apple Intelligence can already access things like Messages and Mail. The defining difference here is trust. Apple Intelligence, at present, attempts to process much of the request on-device.

That's a big reason why Apple Intelligence is relegated to more-powerful Apple chips.

In the event that something does need to be processed off-device, Apple says that only the relevant data is sent to Private Cloud Compute.

We're entering an era where privacy does not exist. At one point, the stock advice to people who were concerned about this very thing was "Well, if you don't like it, don't use it.

But that doesn't protect you anymore. Muse can get access to your information via people who do use it. Apple has made Apple Intelligence non-optional on compatible devices.

This is it, dear reader. You don't get to opt out anymore.

items.title: Making millions of iPhone Duos is proving harder than Apple hoped
items.content_html:
Only Apple knows what it expected for yields, but manufacturers are claiming that the iPhone Duo is difficult to manufacture at scale, with its folding screen and hinge complicating production.

Assembly yields for the iPhone Duo remain low, while component delays have shortened the time available to refine production. Apple now faces a familiar foldable phone problem: producing millions of units that reliably work.

Foxconn's iPhone Duo assembly yield is just above 60%, according to supply chain sources speaking to Jiemian News. The first production batch is small, and the line still needs repeated adjustments.

One source estimated that yields could take six months to a year to mature under Apple's current standards. How this will affect shipping times remains to be seen, but we expect significant delays.

The sources said the low yield does not stem from a single unresolved technical problem. Equipment, processes, and production settings need refinement as the line moves toward larger volumes.

Samsung Display's OLED panels and hinge components made by other manufacturers have also faced insufficient yields and delayed deliveries. Each upstream delay leaves less time for Foxconn to improve assembly yields.

And, as expected, the very thing that makes the iPhone Duo a duo is responsible for many delays: the hinge.

The hinge contains more than 100 parts working together under tight tolerances. Even relatively small differences can wildly affect how the device functions.

Apple reportedly reconsidered using liquid metal in some hinge parts before mass production, but ultimately decided on a different solution. If it were to revise the process, it would require new prototypes and functional samples, verification, and supplier adjustments.

Historically, Apple has considered manufacturing yields an assembler issue. It's not clear what Apple was expecting for a percentage of devices off the line passing quality inspections.

Apple could, theoretically, relax its standards to allow for more saleable units, but that seems improbable. The supplier could also push its production line harder, though it would likely lead to more units completed, but at a higher percentage of defective units.

Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo as part of its "Surprise and Shine" Apple Event on September 12; it starts at an eye-watering $1,999, before taxes. Apple set October 16 for preorders and October 23 for release, which was notably longer after the initial announcement than even the iPhone X.

items.title: Final Cut Pro 13 leaks ahead of announcement with several new features
items.content_html:
A YouTuber has accidentally revealed at least some of what is coming in the Final Cut Pro 13 update, including improved Pixelmator Pro round-tripping and a new Natural Motion Blur tool.

Final Cut Pro 12.4 was released on September 29 with the ability to add Cinematic mode effects captured with iPhone 18 Pro. Apple's next update could arrive sometime in October, given a recent accidental YouTube posting.

Reddit user Sweaty_Succotash_375 pointed out that YouTuber The Final Cut Bro accidentally posted then made a video private that touted "Final Cut 13 is here!" User umChiled shared a chapter list, which shows what features can be expected in the new update.

Here are the features called out in the chapter markers:

Several of these features appear to be long-awaited updates for Final Cut Pro. It's a big update going to version 13, so Apple included several big changes.

It is already possible to send a frame to Pixelmator Pro, but only as a still image for editing. The new roundtrip improvement isn't an export, but a frame editing tool that reinserts what you've edited.

Natural Motion Blur and Keyframe Easing both appear to be big features. Several animation tools have been added, which could mean vastly improved controls over objects in scenes.

Apple hasn't announced Final Cut Pro 13, but new Macs, like a touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED, are expected before the end of 2026. Expect the new Final Cut Pro update to be revealed at the same time.

items.title: GrayKey might have a workaround for Apple's iPhone reboot protection
items.content_html:
It's easier to crack an iPhone after it's been unlocked once by the user after a reboot. A law enforcement tool vendor may have found a way to keep the device in that state.

Magnet Forensics claims its tools preserve iPhone data that Apple's security features would otherwise make harder to access. The tools could give police more time to extract sensitive information from seized devices.

In iOS 18.1, Apple introduced a new privacy feature, a sort of inactivity reboot. This reboot restarts an iPhone after 72 hours without an unlock, returning it to a Before First Unlock (BFU) state.

That state restricts access to encryption keys. As a result, it makes it much harder for anyone to break into an iPhone using brute-force or other methods.

Now, a law enforcement educational video seen by 404 Media details a device called GrayKey Preserve. Magnet also offers Evidence Preservation Mode for its existing GrayKey hardware, which police use to access locked smartphones.

In the video, which was dated early 2025, Magnet says GrayKey Preserve keeps the device in the more accessible After First Unlock (AFU) state, even if an iPhone reboots. Evidence Preservation Mode also reportedly prevents cached locations, recently deleted photos, and iMessages from expiring, preserving them indefinitely.

After initial access, GrayKey Preserve disables cellular, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi connections to isolate the phone from incoming communications. Evidence Preservation Mode then allows law enforcement to effectively freeze the data while waiting for authorization to attempt retrieval.

The video doesn't explain how the feature works. But, iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen believes it could be clock manipulation. It could also disable iPhone tasks that set data to expire.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro review: A massive camera update is just the beginning
items.content_html:
In a year with no base model and a new very high-end model, the iPhone 18 Pro has a lot to prove. After a few weeks testing it, pro and average users alike will find a lot to love.

For the fall 2026 event, Apple mixed things up. Instead of introducing a new base phone, a new iPhone Air, and two new Pros, Apple debuted the two Pros and the iPhone Duo.

Although the iPhone Duo has yet to launch, its announcement may affect purchase plans among prospective iPhone 18 Pro buyers. A new iPhone Air, meanwhile, isn't expected until early 2027.

Here, I'm going to be digging deep into the iPhone 18 Pro. I have the 256GB model in black, though it's also available in 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB capacities.

I'd call this an "S" year iPhone, borrowing a term from the era of two-year phone contracts. Back then, Apple alternated between major redesigns and years focused on performance upgrades.

In performance-upgrade years, Apple kept the phone's overall design and focused on improving its internals. That pattern appeared with the iPhone 3G and 3GS, iPhone 4 and 4S, and iPhone X and XS.

That cadence isn't as relevant as it used to be, but it's what you can expect when going into the iPhone 18 Pro. It has basically the same design as the iPhone 17 Pro with a lot of internal changes.

iPhone 18 Pro review: iPhone 18 Pro has the same 6.3-inch display

You can choose either the iPhone 18 Pro with a 6.3-inch display or the iPhone 18 Pro Max with a 6.9-inch display. Here, I'm focusing on the smaller of the two, and we've broken out the iPhone 18 Pro Max into a separate review.

iPhone 18 Pro comes in four colors this year. You can pick between an updated silver, a matte black, Glacier, or burgundy.

I've been using the black model, with silver and burgundy versions also available in the studio. After seeing all four colors at the unveiling, I found it difficult to choose a favorite.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The new iPhone 18 Pro silver (right) compared to the old iPhone 17 Pro (left)

I usually prefer lighter finishes, and both Glacier and silver stood out to me. The black finish grew on me with use.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The matte black iPhone 18 Pro

The finish is very dark, with glass that matches the rest of the phone. It also readily shows fingerprints, which can leave the body looking smudged.

Fortunately, fingerprints wipe off easily, and it bothered me less than I thought. Since the body is aluminum, I do expect to see some wear marks, such as around the camera plateau, after a year of regular use with no case.

iPhone 18 Pro review: iPhone 18 Pro in Apple's TechWoven case

On the left side of the phone, you have the Action Button above the volume controls. The right side has the sleep/wake button and the Camera Control.

The metal body wraps around the back, giving way to a piece of glass that affords 25W MagSafe wireless charging. On the camera plateau, there is a trio of 48MP cameras (ultra-wide, main, and telephoto), the TrueTone flash, and a LiDAR that can aid focus.

On the bottom, you have the USB-C port, which supports fast data transfers and charging.

Not much has changed with the display this time around. It's the same size, though Apple did put the Face ID infrared camera behind the display.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The under-screen IR camera that is used for Face ID is now in the top-left corner

The IR camera is in the top-left corner, and you can see it if you look for it under the right lighting. Some users have said that Face ID has been problematic for them and blame the new under-screen IR camera.

I can say that in my few weeks with the iPhone 18 Pro, I've never had Face ID fail on me. That makes me think that if this is an issue, it's limited and perhaps software-related.

Apple has already rolled out iOS 27.0.1, fixing one Face ID issue on the new devices. What I do believe will impact Face ID now are certain screen protectors.

Matte anti-glare screen protectors typically leave a cutout or glossy section over the Face ID camera. Early versions appear incompatible with the relocated camera, suggesting accessory makers weren't prepared for the change.

By relocating the IR camera to the corner, Apple was able to shrink the Dynamic Island. Since it's smaller, you can now track up to three Live Activities at once.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The new Dynamic Island is smaller and supports 3 Live Activities

So far, I haven't noticed this much. There are times when I have three Live Activities, but it isn't as useful as I thought it would be.

It's a nice-to-have, but don't expect to be overly thrilled with the slightly smaller size.

The screen retains Apple's Ceramic Shield 2 coating, which has impressed me with its scratch resistance. I previously criticized the fine scratches that accumulated on my screen after just a few months of use.

Ceramic Shield 2 on my iPhone 17 Pro held up so well that my screen was completely pristine after a whole year. That's with keys, coins, and other stuff in my pocket that used to damage the display.

Since it has the same finish here, I expect the glass to hold up just as well.

Otherwise, it's Apple's typical great display tech. An always-on Super Retina XDR panel with a 2,000,000-to-1 contrast ratio, 1000 nits of usual brightness, and 3000 nits of peak outdoor brightness.

It has ProMotion for adjustable frame rates that intelligently go up to 120Hz when needed. It looks fantastic.

Not specific to iPhone 18 Pro are Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Like iPhone 17 Pro, there are a few somewhat exclusive features, like the customizable Siri voice that gets processed on device.

Much of Siri's AI processing uses Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC), so general performance has felt largely unchanged. Siri answers general knowledge questions just as quickly as before.

If I had one spot that was quicker, it's with Visual Intelligence, or what is now the new Siri mode in the Camera app. Just long-press the Camera Control and the Camera app will launch straight into Siri mode.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Using Siri AI to diagnose my apples

It was faster to recognize objects and start processing them before I tried to do anything. Scanning the apples in my backyard, it was able to diagnose the blemishes in only a second or two.

Apple Intelligence touches so many facets of your phone. Things like deep indexing of all your messages, emails, calls, calendars, notes, and apps to answer questions, Extend and Reframe in Photos, or the new Writing Tools.

There is Image Playground, Live Translation, deep world knowledge, HomeKit Secure Video camera analysis, and more that all live under the umbrella term. I think Apple Intelligence is becoming a lot more useful, and iOS 27 has put a lot of polish into these intelligent features.

There are a few areas where I start to see speed improvements, at least when it can be handled on the device. Using Genmoji took a second and a half to create an iced latte emoji on my iPhone 18 Pro, but it took about 3 seconds on my iPhone 17 Pro.

I'm certain Apple is going to keep adding Apple Intelligence features throughout iOS, so I think we'll continue to see better performance as those show up.

For the iPhone 18 Pro, it can charge wirelessly via MagSafe or Qi2 at up to 25W. If you prefer wired, Apple has boosted the speed, and it can now support up to 60W of input power instead of maxing out at 40W.

The phone also officially supports AVS, or Adjustable Voltage Supply. An AVS charger will increase to a higher wattage before settling down at a lower one and can adjust in smaller intervals.

Typical chargers have preset outputs that they go between, whereas an AVS charger is more granular and can tailor the input speeds second by second to what your phone needs.

With a compatible charger, you can charge the battery to 50% in just 15 minutes. That makes a quick top-up useful when your battery runs low during the day.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Placing iPhone 18 Pro on a MagSafe charger

I primarily use MagSafe, so I rarely plug my phone in to charge. Wired charging proved faster during testing, but the improvement hasn't felt essential for my routine.

What I liked more was the increase in battery life. Apple says for video playback, the phone has increased from 33 hours to 36 hours.

iPhone 18 Pro review: StandBy mode on a MagSafe charger

I'm a heavy user since I'm constantly posting short-form videos to socials, and I was used to charging frequently. I have noticed a difference and have started to have less fear about my phone dying early.

The iPhone 18 Pro runs on Apple's latest A20 Pro processor. It's the first iPhone chip manufactured using a 2nm process.

The 2nm process improves performance and power efficiency across the phone. The chip has a six-core CPU with two super cores and four efficiency cores.

This is the first time Apple is using super cores on its iPhone chip after first debuting on the Mac. The GPU has 7 cores and has new Neural Accelerators.

Additionally, we get dual 16-core Neural Engines. It's a big improvement year-over-year for intensive tasks.

As in recent years, you're unlikely to notice much improvement in everyday use. Even substantial speed gains make little difference when opening apps, browsing social media, or checking email.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Geekbench 7 single-core results

I did start to notice it with anything that pushed the silicon. Launching games was quicker, as was running complex shortcuts.

My iPhone 17 Pro took 24 seconds to launch a new game of Civ VII, and my iPhone 18 Pro was way faster at 15 seconds. This was on high quality, standard color, and identical game settings.

In the Photos app, using the on-device fast version of the Clean Up tool, the iPhone 18 Pro took 3 seconds compared to 5 seconds for the identical task on the iPhone 17 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Geekbench results on iPhone 18 Pro

In Geekbench 7 benchmarks, iPhone 18 Pro scored 3927 for the single-core, up significantly from the 3168 my iPhone 17 Pro scored, both on iOS 27.2 beta. The multi-core went from 8258 to 10462.

That's more than a 24% improvement for the single-core and almost a 27% improvement for the multi-core. It's no surprise that the iPhone 18 Pro feels so much faster in these prolonged tasks.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Geekbench 7 multi-core results

Not only are we seeing higher scores in benchmarks, but sustained performance is better thanks to the next-generation vapor chamber. Apple says it has a larger surface area as well as more conductive material.

This has caused the phone to feel hot at times, but that's partially by design. Aluminum is great at conducting heat, so the more efficient liquid cooling is pulling that heat from the internal components and using the aluminum to dissipate that heat.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Graphics got a huge jump for iPhone 18 Pro

On the graphics side, Geekbench 7 Metal test earned 61961 on iPhone 18 Pro and 42465 on iPhone 17 Pro.

Between the improved cooling and new chip, this is one of the largest generational improvements we've seen on iPhone.

Despite a slew of software-related changes, the headlining feature for the camera is Apple's impressive variable aperture main lens. Six exceptionally thin blades come together to control how much light is able to hit the camera's sensor.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The variable aperture closed (left) and open (right) on the main lens

Aperture can be a confusing thing, and not just because making it smaller, or lower in value, will increase the background bokeh while simultaneously shrinking the depth of the in-focus area. It's typically been more of a "pro" control for DSLR and mirrorless cameras.

Almost everyone can benefit from this feature, even without manually adjusting the aperture.

Compared to the iPhone 17 Pro, Apple was able to increase the overall aperture from an f/1.78 to an f/1.48. Apple likely would have been happy to do this before, but it presented obstacles.

If the main aperture was widened to a fixed f/1.48, certain shots would result in too much unintended blur. People in group photos often stand at different distances from the camera.

A fixed f/1.48 aperture creates a shallow depth of field, which can leave some faces out of focus.

What Apple was able to achieve here is a faster (wider) aperture, but made it adjustable. Group shots will keep everyone in focus with a higher aperture like an f/4.0, but solo portraits or low-light shots can move to an f/1.48 to allow more light in and have more stylized background bokeh.

You'll still benefit if you leave the camera in automatic mode and never adjust the aperture yourself. For certain photos and videos, the camera automatically selects f/1.48 to improve image quality.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Comparing the f/1.48 to f/4.0 aperture differences

Since the launch, I've seen a lot of people suggesting there is little to no difference in their photos going from the iPhone 17 Pro to the iPhone 18 Pro, and they're likely not wrong. They're just comparing the wrong photos.

The only real change in the camera hardware is the variable aperture, so it's only in shots that benefit from a faster aperture that you'll see improvements in the photos.

For me, the first thing I noticed in taking photos of my kids is that it doesn't switch to Night Mode as frequently. The wider aperture allows in more light, reducing the requirement to switch into the long-shutter Night Mode.

Even in the past few weeks, trying to take photos of my kids when we're playing in their room before bed, it's been great. Kids don't stay still, especially when playing, so I've got a lot of photos I wouldn't have been able to get just a month ago.

When taking photos in New York City after sundown, I also noticed improvement in photos when directly comparing the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro. Sometimes the noise reduction on the iPhone 17 Pro was too aggressive, resulting in some deformities in objects, like warped window panes.

Some of these changes may be because of the faster aperture, but some could be attributed to the A20 Pro image signal processor (ISP) as well.

It is pixel peeping to a degree, but it's a measurable improvement generation-to-generation. If you ever plan on cropping in any low-light photos, those small details matter more.

The last thing you'll notice is less blur in photos. Since the aperture can be wider and allow more light in, it allows the shutter speed to increase and capture the same shot.

That's why sometimes lower/wider apertures are called "faster." Looking at kiddos again, a faster shutter will mean sharper images more often.

If you compare a shot of your backyard during the day with the iPhone 17 Pro and compare it to the iPhone 18 Pro, you likely will not see a difference. But for average users, the difference can be real in the right scenarios.

For pro users, things can go further. I thoroughly enjoyed stepping down the aperture to f/1.48 when taking photos of food, my kids, tech gadgets in the studio, and more.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The new manual controls for the variable aperture

You can see the difference easily when adjusting between the f/1.48 and f/4.0 that are made available. If you happen to use a third-party camera app like the Moment Pro Camera, you can get even more granular with 1/3 f-stops instead of the four predefined ones Apple offers.

One thing I've loved doing is stepping up the aperture to an f/2.8 or f/4.0 for low-light shots. Because of the new blades that slide in front of the lens, this causes starburst effects to appear on light sources.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Slow shutter and an f/4.0 created blur in the street and starburst effects on the lights

Some may not like this, but I love it. It makes something coming out of your iPhone feel more like something off of a dedicated camera.

To be clear, the variable aperture is not going to give you the same degree of bokeh as a real camera with a full-size sensor due to the tiny size of the sensor. But it isn't a gimmick, and I think it's one of the bigger upgrades Apple has added to the Camera in years.

If I'm being honest with myself, I rarely use Photographic Styles. I should say, I used to rarely use them.

The new iPhone 18 Pro changed that.

Apple is releasing the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max with Photographic Styles 3, and it's a big change. In addition to a change in how you adjust them that will arrive on older devices, the newest ones gain texture.

Photographic Styles, available alongside all other camera controls, can be persistent and applied to all photos you take, or adjusted on a one-off basis. This is a toggle in the Settings app.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Black and white shot from iPhone 18 Pro with film style

If you choose one of the many styles, you can slide your finger up and down and left and right on a grid to adjust the tone and color, respectively. If you drag your finger below the grid, you can adjust the intensity of the style from 0 to 100.

The big new additions are the textures, which live in a separate tab within each style. You can choose between soft skin, glow, and film, and each of these can have grain applied.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Apple's new skin softening texture, which works decently well even with a beard

The soft skin effect is popular in apps like FaceTune. It adds a slight blur or softening to skin, which can be flattering.

Glow is more subtle, adding a very slight glowing effect to subjects. This one could be more aggressive, but Apple typically doesn't like to overly distort photos.

iPhone 18 Pro review: A night shot of 30 Rock with the film style and grain applied

The last texture is film, which is my favorite. I love shooting on my Nikon Zf, which has film effects and is amazing for summer beaches, fall landscapes, or black and white cityscapes.

Combining the film effect with the grain is a winning combo for me, and I love the sample shots I took with it. I think Apple should update this to allow more control over the grain, such as size and amount, but this is an excellent first implementation.

iPhone 18 Pro review: A low-light shot of a street vendor with the black and white film style applied

I've used this feature far more often than earlier versions of Photographic Styles, enabling it for a variety of shots. It's useful enough that I expect to keep using it regularly.

Aside from the new faster aperture and new Photographic Styles 3, Apple also baked in a slew of software enhancements that are exclusive to the new devices. The biggest and most meaningful of those changes is what Apple is calling Pro Controls.

Pro Controls is a collection of manual camera settings that, until now, would have required users to download a third-party app. There's nothing wrong with that, but it's also great to see these integrated into the stock offering.

Perhaps, in part, the fruit of former Halide developer Sebastiaan de With, who Apple officially hired at the beginning of 2026. As part of the design team, he surely had some impact here.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Customizable controls on iPhone 18 Pro

These controls consist of the aforementioned manual aperture, shutter speed, focus, and white balance. You can toggle on a histogram, too.

The controls are very well thought out and simple to use. My only gripe is that none of these new controls are available on the Camera Control.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The Camera Control on iPhone 18 Pro

Apple's touch-sensitive button persists, and I remain adamant that it is the best way to open the Camera app, and often the best way to take photos. Sometimes the touch controls can be fiddly, but they can always be disabled.

I'm one who uses the Camera Control usually for zoom, but I think sliding my finger to control the aperture would be my new go-to and seems a natural fit here. It seems trivial for Apple to have included them, regardless of whether it plans to remove the touch sensitivity in future versions.

Using these controls, you can get some amazing shots from the iPhone 18 Pro. My personal favorite as of late has been the shutter speed. If you prolong the shutter, you can take these long-exposure shots with blurred movement.

iPhone 18 Pro review: I love this photo I shot of Radio City Music Hall with the blurred taxis in the foreground

In New York City, I got a series of shots in front of Radio City Music Hall with cars and taxis blurring past in the foreground. My kids playing with glow sticks was also really fun to photograph.

White balance has historically been a pain for me on mobile. On my primary camera, I always set a fixed white balance because, depending on what I am shooting, it can adjust mid-shoot and ruin the shot.

Imagine shooting a set of AirPods with the white case, and they go from blue to yellow based on the background and lights in the room. It's frustrating, to say the least, and I'd have to lock the white balance when locking the exposure and focus beforehand.

Apple gives you five preset white balances to choose from: tungsten, cloudy, fluorescent, daylight, and shadow. Each of these has its corresponding Kelvin value displayed.

iPhone 18 Pro review: A slow manual shutter let me capture the nice blur on the water fountain

Other apps give you an actual slider to dial in the Kelvin value to exactly what you want, but the presets will be good enough for most users.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that the manual focus was more than meets the eye. Instead of simply giving you a dial that you can use to change the focus, Apple went further.

The interface breaks the system down into its three individual cameras. You can now manually choose whether you're shooting with the ultra-wide, main, or telephoto.

It seems counterintuitive, but this is something you could not do in the default Camera app before. Sometimes you thought you were using the telephoto, but you weren't.

If you would zoom in, the app would intelligently determine which camera to use — a cropped version of the main camera or the telephoto lens.

Sometimes, cropping in the main sensor in lower light is preferable to switching the dedicated telephoto lens. But the focus control specifically lets you choose between the three and adjust the focus for them.

When you adjust the focus, it includes focus peaking. As you slide your finger on the focus control, the image dims and the in-focus part of the image will outline in white.

That way, you can tell instantly which part of the frame you're focusing on. It's very useful.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Taking pics with the new iPhone 18 Pro camera system

Speaking of focus, that is something else that has greatly improved. Apple now has true subject tracking autofocus.

In both photo and video modes, you can double-tap on a subject. As that subject moves, the focus will follow it.

iPhone 18 Pro review: Subject tracking keeps the focus even if they move off-screen and back

This persists even if the subject moves off-screen, which is great for kids or sports. It worked well, though it did take a moment or so to lock back on at times when the subject returned to the frame.

To help make these controls easier to access, the Camera app is now customizable. The good news is that this customizable interface will come to older phones, even if they don't have the Pro Controls.

I pinned the stuff I use most right at the top of the interface, such as the aperture, shutter speed, styles, and focus. They're quick to access, though I hope Apple expands the interface options down the line with additional placement positions.

Somehow, Apple has many more camera features I haven't touched on or played around with enough yet. Cinematic mode, for example, can now apply the blur after the fact to any video you capture, not just in the dedicated Cinematic shooting mode.

There are new options for audio mix, which is designed for music and can boost singing alongside the instrumentation. Everyone's Grayson Smith piano videos from Disney World are going to be even better now!

Timelapse videos can now be filmed in 4K with Dolby Vision HDR. They have stabilization now too, which will help for brief handheld shoots.

Finally, Apple introduced Reference Image. This is off by default, but cryptographically ties an image to your exact phone at the time of capture.

I think the main example of this would be photojournalism. You'll know a photo was unaltered and taken on an iPhone and not something AI-generated.

This only works on the main lens, and Apple describes it as a secure digital negative. When you take a picture, you'll have the photo and the reference image stored in your Camera Roll.

When you share the photo, if anyone debates the authenticity, you can verify it against the Reference Image. When Reference Image is turned on, you need to shoot in the new Reference mode, and only some effects, like Live Photos, Portraits, and Photographic Styles, will work.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple delivered a stellar upgrade. Even from iPhone 17 Pro, there are a lot of things that I appreciate.

Not to say I'm advocating for everyone with an iPhone 17 Pro to upgrade, though. A lot of people may not notice these differences, like if they aren't doing a ton on their phone, don't use Apple Intelligence features, don't go through battery life, and don't take a ton of photos.

For me, this is a huge "S" year upgrade, and it feels like Apple is listening to its users. This upgrade focused heavily on camera, performance/heat, and battery.

The number of camera changes is huge. We get new Pro Controls, Photographic Styles 3 with textures, next-gen Cinematic mode after capture, Reference Images, variable aperture, improved low-light performance, better audio mix, and more.

Multi-core performance is up over 27%, with sustained performance up to 40% better. Even average users are going to start noticing load times being faster.

Battery on the base Pro is longer than it's ever been, and new faster charging helps you keep it there. These are all great changes to see for the iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro review: The black color looks striking

My complaints are fairly minimal, like missing the vibrant Cosmic Orange color and the lack of the Camera Control. They certainly wouldn't stop me from buying this phone.

The only reason not to recommend this is if you're debating the iPhone Duo. But that comparison is for another time.

items.title: Home Hub will rely on AI to identify which user's content to display
items.content_html:
Apple's forthcoming Home Hub is already expected to tailor its display and data to different users, but now it appears it will do so using AI facial recognition instead of Face ID.

The long-expected Home Hub, or HomePod with a screen, is now expected to be launched on October 13, 2026, and more details including colors are continuing to leak out in advance. Now in Bloomberg's new "Power On" podcast, it's claimed that the device will use AI facial recognition.

It's been expected since the very first rumors of the device that it would present different content for different users in a household. So depending on which family member is using the device, they would automatically get their photos, music, calendar events, and so on.

That's likely to be done in part by the device looking for iPhones in the proximity, but it's also been presumed that it would use Face ID to identify the current user. Now according to Bloomberg, there will be exactly this user-switching and there will be facial recognition, but not Face ID.

The AI facial recognition technology to be used is described only as being highly technical, and there is no explanation for why it isn't Face ID. Extrapolating from other Apple Home system leaks, it's possible that this is the same technology that will be used in future security cameras.

Rather than either scanning a face when someone stands in front of the sensor, such a system could continuously monitor its environment. In the case of the security camera system, it could do this and only trigger recordings when activity is spotted.

So perhaps the Home Hub will constantly monitor its surroundings but only actively identify a user when that person interacts with it from anywhere in the room.

The same report also repeats earlier claims that Apple has had this device manufactured and ready to ship for a considerable time. It's believed that its launch was held back while Apple waited for the improved Siri AI to be released.

Also about to be released is the updated MacBook Pro, currently expected in October or November. This same podcast report also repeats an earlier expectation that this MacBook Pro will be the first to feature a Dynamic Island.

items.title: Apple's home camera will tell you who's home without showing video footage
items.content_html:
Beyond the Home Hub, Apple's rumored home camera peripheral is rumored to just describe household activity without giving users or hackers video footage to watch.

The device, code-named J450, is designed to complement Apple's upcoming HomeHub. It would provide text updates about people and pets instead of letting users access a video feed.

On Thursday's episode of the Power On podcast, Mark Gurman described the device as a cylinder that "looks like a metal giant...chapstick." He said its camera would operate at a low frame rate, using AI to analyze its surroundings without recording video.

Facial recognition would let the device identify who entered a room or left the house. The device would also be able to identify pets.

It seems as though Apple could position the device as a privacy-focused alternative to conventional home security cameras. However, Gurman's comments did not establish where images would be processed.

Apple's HomeHub is expected to be revealed on October 13. Current rumors suggest that it will be a tablet-like device that is carried from room to room, but that's not at all clear yet.

items.title: Oppo can't get accusations of Apple Watch trade secret theft dismissed
items.content_html:
A federal judge didn't buy Oppo's OpenAI-like arguments about IP theft by an engineer that allegedly took Apple Watch trade secrets to Oppo.

In August 2025, Apple accused ex-employee Chen Shi of sharing confidential Apple Watch details with Chinese rival Oppo. According to Courthouse News, he is accused of having done so in order to secure a job with what US District Judge Eumi Lee calls "a generous salary."

Now Judge Lee has ruled that the case can proceed. Specifically, she said that Apple's claims of breach of contract alone are sufficient that she would not dismiss the case.

In her six-page ruling, Judge Lee uses the word "plausibly" to describe Apple's allegations 14 times. In a similar move to OpenAI in its current case with Apple, Oppo argued that the information in question was not a trade secret.

Judge Lee ruled that Apple has made specific allegations concerning at least one trade secret.

Oppo's argument was also that Apple uses the term trade secret so broadly that Shi "cannot practice as an engineer in the health-sensing field without violating it."

Judge Lee disagreed, saying that the Intellectual Property Agreement (IPA) that Shi signed with Apple only precludes him from disclosing confidential company information.

As detailed in the ruling, Apple alleges that, "late at night just three days before leaving Apple, Dr Shi downloaded 63 documents," which he transferred to a USB drive. Prior to leaving, he also "set up and attended dozens of one-on-one meetings with Apple Watch technical team members to learn about their ongoing research."

Separately, it's been alleged that Shi told Apple he was leaving to care for family members, and not that he was joining Oppo. He's also accused of having searched online for ways to cover up his actions, such as searching for "can somebody see if I've opened a file on a shared drive."

Oppo is not a well-known name in the US. But, its smartwatches are a key rival to the Apple Watch in China.

Defendants Guangdong Oppo Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Ltd. and InnoPeak Technology, Inc. now have until October 21, 2026, to file a responsive pleading. That means filing specific defenses against Apple's allegations.

That's significant because up to now, Oppo has reportedly failed to cooperate with discovery. The court ordered Oppo to comply by October 31, 2025.

There was also a deadline for Shi to take part in a deposition, but he asked for it to be extended. Reportedly around this time he had been diagnosed with a condition that could worsen if he were in "a lengthy, high-stress, and adversarial proceeding."

It's not clear whether that deposition has been rescheduled. It does appear, though, that Oppo has continued to delay complying with the discovery order.

That delay is not part of the new ruling about Apple having plausible reason to sue. Separately, Apple claimed in March 2026 that it needed an emergency injunction to prevent Oppo deleting evidence.

Judge Lee is reportedly still considering this request. What's most likely to happen next, then, is that she will rule over that preliminary injunction.

Other than the October 21, 2026 deadline for responsive pleading, no further dates regarding the case have been published.

Judge Lee is also presiding over a separate iCloud case. In 2025, she ruled in favor of consumers pressing for a case to be heard against Apple.

items.title: Apple Vision Pro's development graveyard exemplifies Apple's '1,000 no's to every yes'
items.content_html:
Pundits continue to hold up clear signs of restraint as failures while asking Apple to behave like Meta, OpenAI, Google, or anyone else but themselves, especially when discussing Apple Vision Pro.

If any of Apple's thousands of employees dare leave the company, or if one of hundreds of internal prototypes doesn't make it to production, you better believe punditry will be there to let us know.

The critical analysis almost always suffers from the same problem: asking Apple to chase the puck to where it is today, not where it is going.

Look, there are a dozen Steve Jobs-isms that I can throw in here that should tell you exactly how Apple operates. It is one of the most scrutinized companies on Earth, and yet, reporting in the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg can't help but ask Apple to change its behavior.

That Apple essence may confound analysts and pontificators, but one thing has held true in its long history: don't bet against it.

The focus of the week is on Meta's new "VR Glasses" that are neither VR nor glasses. Sure, they weigh 1/6 less and cost 1/3 the price, but they're also half the spec.

Apple Vision Pro has a weight problem, absolutely, but let us not pretend that Apple is actually okay with sacrificing fidelity and scope for that simple metric. Even this report shows the lengths of the research and prototyping Apple went through to try and get a smaller device sooner, but chose to say "no."

But of course, in light of Meta's "yes" with Meta VR Glasses, Apple's no's need to be seen as a failure. I'll let Apple's 2013 WWDC introduction video do the talking on this one (if it isn't taken down).

I mean, given the reporting from folks who have spent many long years in the industry, it seems they forget exactly who they are talking about.

Apple has an untold number of active prototypes in development and magnitudes more in a graveyard out back. I have no doubt that Apple's secret projects division is working on everything from rollable OLED to drones.

That doesn't mean we'll ever see any of these products, nor does it mean that every abandoned prototype is a sign of failure and mismanagement. Every time a project is canceled in spite of the sunk cost, that is a victory.

But apparently three known abandoned internal prototypes are a sign of confusion, failure, and mismanagement.

These are likely three of dozens of prototypes being conceptualized at Apple Park. What is interesting is that instead of fast-tracking one of the other potential designs in the 28-month interval between the M2 model's reveal and the M5 model's launch, Apple stuck with what it had.

Meta VR Glasses are an example of what a compromised product might look like. Lower resolution, lower fidelity, lower field of view — clearly Apple didn't want this even if it could build it.

What's interesting is the "failure" narrative about Apple Vision Pro assumes a lot that we don't know. No one outside of Apple knows the success metric for the product or if Apple is meeting that.

Apple Car is one of Apple's biggest no's

Capturing a quarter of Meta's VR headset revenue in a single holiday quarter in spite of an entrenched market doesn't sound like a failure to me.

Also, CEO John Ternus is apparently supposed to dislike the whole project and has reportedly "put it on ice." Meanwhile, his press tours have revealed only positive talk of the product, insisting that unique use cases like surgeons using the product are why Apple is in this business.

However, the reports want us to view this as a reason to dislike Apple Vision Pro.

Life-changing medical procedures aren't enough, no. We need this thing to sell in the tens of millions to matter.

Even with the Apple Vision Pro team reportedly "on ice" they are busy developing a "revamped" N224 that could be the true successor to Apple Vision Pro. There are about four prototypes being tested, and one that even uses an external compute block like Meta VR Glasses.

Apple didn't pivot, it doubled down on its hardware and spec combination until technology caught up

That's how Meta apparently "beat" Apple to market with a device that doesn't launch until spring at $1,299. Early reports suggest it works fine, but the lack of light shields and more limited field of view and fidelity make it a worse experience.

But of course, Meta apparently "demonstrated" that Apple's execution was the problem all along with the Apple Vision Pro. Yes, that's definitely it, as long as you ignore the successes of the headset, how it has influenced the market, and how Apple Vision Pro was a clear template for Meta's latest hardware.

It wasn't enough that Meta basically cloned visionOS for its Meta Quest line and mixed reality prototypes. Nope, the company even hired former Apple design chief Alan Dye to help nail down that Apple look and feel.

But I'm confused. I thought we were all meant to dislike the guy for Liquid Glass, but now it's apparently Meta's victory for poaching him.

I guess as long as it's a failure for Apple, reporting will choose whatever narrative best fits that mold.

The inconsistent reporting around Apple Vision Pro has been incredible. It's dead, it's not, it's dead again, development is halted, it's going again but on life support.

Apple Vision Pro is the template spatial computing is being built on, but that's still a 'failure' apparently

Analysts and pundits need Apple Vision Pro to fail for whatever reason. That's why every product even close to AR/VR/MR has been deemed an "Apple Vision Pro killer."

Either this thing is dead and a failure, or it's one hell of a resilient product in spite of poor punditry. I think I'll go with the latter until I see the gravestone.

Apple's regular employee churn and reconfigurations internally don't show anything but business as usual. As far as AppleInsider has been able to uncover, development continues, albeit slowly, as Apple waits for technology to catch up with Apple's vision of the next-generation headset.

Remember, Apple Vision Pro's only true problems are its high starting price and lack of developer support. Everything else is just opinion and conjecture.
